plan.question: Does the new checkout increase the conversion rate?
plan.estimand: Difference in the share of sessions that convert, treatment minus control, in percentage points, across all genuine sessions in the 14-day experiment (ratio of converted sessions in treatment minus in control, times 100), with a two-sided 95% interval from a regression that clusters on user_id.

decision_rule.metric: conversion lift, treatment minus control (percentage points)

columns.name: session_id
columns.note: unique id of the checkout session; one row per session

columns.name: user_id
columns.note: id of the user; a user has 1 to 4 sessions and the variant is assigned per user

columns.name: day
columns.note: day of the 14-day experiment, integers 0 to 13

columns.name: variant
columns.note: experiment arm, exactly 'treatment' or 'control'; the estimand is treatment minus control

columns.name: platform
columns.note: platform of the session: web, ios or android

columns.name: is_internal
columns.note: True for sessions of internal staff or test users, who are not genuine customers

columns.name: session_seconds
columns.note: session length in seconds; very short sessions are bot-like

columns.name: converted
columns.note: 1 if the session ended in a purchase, else 0; the outcome

columns.name: revenue
columns.note: revenue of the session; 0 unless converted is 1

steps.title: Whether to drop internal staff and test sessions
steps.description: is_internal marks sessions of staff or test users who are not genuine customers, so including them can bias the lift. Keeping them is a legitimate choice only if the aim is all traffic.

options.label: Drop internal sessions
options.rationale: Only genuine customers are relevant to whether the checkout converts customers better.
options.spec: Keep only rows where is_internal is False (drop rows where is_internal is True). Write nothing to ctx. Return the filtered frame.
options.source: Experiment hygiene convention

options.label: Keep internal sessions
options.rationale: Treats every session as a real checkout attempt, which matches a whole-traffic view of the rollout.
options.spec: Keep all rows, including those where is_internal is True. Write nothing to ctx. Return the frame unchanged.

steps.title: Whether to drop very short, bot-like sessions
steps.description: session_seconds has a minimum of 0.2 s and the column note says very short sessions are bot-like. The threshold for bot-like is a judgement call.

options.label: Keep all session lengths
options.rationale: Does not assume any threshold; bots are assumed to be rare relative to the sample.
options.spec: Keep all rows regardless of session_seconds. Write nothing to ctx. Return the frame unchanged.

options.label: Drop sessions under 2 seconds
options.rationale: Removes implausibly fast sessions that cannot be genuine checkouts.
options.spec: Keep only rows where session_seconds is at least 2.0. Write nothing to ctx. Return the filtered frame.

steps.title: How to handle extreme session lengths
steps.description: session_seconds has extreme values far from the median. Trimming or winsorizing changes the covariate used for adjustment without changing the outcome.

options.label: Use session_seconds as recorded
options.rationale: Keeps every observation; a log transform handles skew without discarding information.
options.spec: Create session_log = log(session_seconds + 1) as a new column, using numpy.log1p. Write nothing to ctx. Return the frame with session_log added.

options.label: Winsorize session_seconds at the 1st and 99th percentiles
options.rationale: Limits the leverage of extreme session lengths while keeping every row.
options.spec: Create session_log = log(clip(session_seconds, p1, p99) + 1), where p1 and p99 are the 1st and 99th percentiles of session_seconds computed on the current frame, using numpy.percentile and numpy.clip. Write nothing to ctx. Return the frame with session_log added.
options.source: Winsorizing convention (Tukey 1977)

steps.title: Covariates to adjust for
steps.description: The adjustment set is chosen here. Randomisation makes adjustment optional, but adjusting for pre-treatment covariates can tighten the interval.

options.label: No covariates
options.rationale: Randomised assignment already balances the arms, so the simplest estimate is unbiased.
options.spec: Set ctx['covariates'] to an empty list. Do not add or drop any columns. Return the frame unchanged.

options.label: Adjust for platform
options.rationale: Platform is pre-treatment and strongly affects checkout conversion, so adjusting can reduce variance.
options.spec: Set ctx['covariates'] to ['platform']. Do not add or drop any columns. Platform is dummy coded by the model step with drop_first=True. Return the frame unchanged.

options.label: Adjust for platform and log session length
options.rationale: Session length is pre-treatment only if measured before exposure; it is included to absorb residual variation in engagement.
options.spec: Set ctx['covariates'] to ['platform', 'session_log']. Do not add or drop any columns. Platform is dummy coded by the model step with drop_first=True. Return the frame unchanged.

steps.title: Estimator for the conversion lift
steps.description: Each option estimates treatment minus control conversion on the same outcome, converted, with a cluster-robust interval on user_id (16000 users, far above 30).

options.label: Linear probability model with user-clustered errors
options.rationale: Gives the lift directly in probability units, which Borges scales to percentage points.
options.spec: Fit statsmodels OLS of converted on an intercept, the indicator variant equal to treatment (1 for treatment, 0 for control), and the covariates in ctx['covariates'] (categorical covariates dummy coded with drop_first=True). Use cluster-robust standard errors clustered on user_id. Return the coefficient on the variant indicator as the estimate, with its 95% confidence interval and two-sided p-value.
options.source: Linear probability model; Abadie et al. on clustered SEs

options.label: Logit with average marginal effect
options.rationale: Models the probability non-linearly and averages the treatment effect over sessions, which stays on the lift scale.
options.spec: Fit statsmodels Logit of converted on an intercept, the indicator variant equal to treatment (1 for treatment, 0 for control), and the covariates in ctx['covariates'] (categorical covariates dummy coded with drop_first=True), using cluster-robust standard errors clustered on user_id. Compute the average marginal effect of the variant indicator over all rows by predicting converted with variant set to 1 and to 0 and taking the mean difference. Return that average marginal effect as the estimate, with a 95% interval and two-sided p-value from the delta method on the cluster-robust covariance.
options.source: Average marginal effects (Ai and Norton 2003)

data.reason: The estimand explicitly targets genuine sessions, and the column notes define is_internal as staff or test users who are not genuine customers, so dropping them is the standard and correct filter for this question. It is the conventional option and is applied as specified.

The estimand is explicitly defined over genuine sessions, and the column notes state that internal sessions are not genuine customers. Keeping them changes the population the question asks about and can bias the lift, so the option is indefensible for this estimand.

Keeping all session lengths is the conventional and a defensible choice: it avoids an arbitrary bot threshold, and the sample is large enough that the few bot-like sessions are unlikely to drive the difference in conversion share. The estimand is over all genuine sessions, and this option keeps the sessions as recorded; a reviewer would accept it, though the bot-like sessions remain a stated risk rather than a checked one.

Winsorizing a covariate at the 1st and 99th percentiles is a standard, defensible way to limit leverage from extreme session lengths while keeping all rows; the outcome is untouched and the estimand (treatment minus control conversion difference) is preserved. It is a reasonable alternative to using the raw covariate that a reviewer would accept with a sentence of justification.

This is the conventional and standard practice: a log1p transform handles the heavy right skew of session length while keeping every observation, and it is a reasonable choice for a covariate that the estimand's outcome does not depend on. It does not change the estimand, and the spec is the conventional one, so it is an accepted choice rather than an alternative that would reproduce a no-op result.

Variant is randomised per user, so an unadjusted difference in conversion shares is an unbiased estimate of the treatment-minus-control effect; the no-covariates option is the standard choice for this estimand, and the interval is handled separately by user-level clustering.

Dropping implausibly short bot-like sessions is a standard data-quality filter for checkout experiments; the threshold of 2 seconds is a reasonable operationalisation of the column note's 'very short sessions are bot-like', and the session_seconds column is described as containing exactly this information. It does not change the estimand, since genuine sessions remain the population of interest, though the choice of threshold is a sensitivity matter.

Platform is a pre-treatment covariate that plausibly drives checkout conversion and is independent of random assignment, so adjusting for it leaves the difference-in-proportions estimand unchanged while potentially tightening the interval. It is a standard, reviewer-acceptable covariate adjustment for a randomised experiment, and it is not equivalent to the no-covariate conventional option since it changes the model specification.

Randomisation makes adjustment optional, and the conventional unadjusted spec is valid; adding platform (pre-treatment, plausibly balanced) is harmless but session_log is measured during the session, which is after exposure to the new checkout and can itself be affected by treatment (a mediator or post-treatment variable), so adjusting for it changes what is estimated. The rationale admits it is included only to absorb residual variation, which is not a valid pre-treatment justification.

A linear probability model with user-clustered errors is the standard way to estimate a difference in conversion shares in percentage points; the variant is assigned per user, so clustering on user_id with 16,000 clusters is appropriate and the coefficient is directly interpretable as the lift in probability units. The option does not address the internal/bot filter, but that belongs to a separate step and does not make the estimator itself indefensible.

A logit average marginal effect with user-clustered delta-method intervals is a standard, reviewer-accepted way to report a binary-outcome treatment effect on the probability scale. It estimates the same lift as the linear probability model (the estimand is unchanged), with 16,000 clusters far above 30, and the covariates are the same as the conventional spec. Because the outcome is binary and the AME stays on the percentage-point scale, it is a reasonable alternative to the linear probability model rather than a change of estimand.

data.problem: The spec says to compute session_log = log(clip(session_seconds, p1, p99) + 1) using numpy.percentile and numpy.clip, but the code uses pandas quantile and Series.clip and calls np.log rather than numpy.log1p. The resulting values are equivalent in principle, so the discrepancy is in the implementation route rather than the computed quantity, and the effects (min 0.617, max 6.586, consistent with clipping at the 1st and 99th percentiles) match the spec. Because the computed values match the intended transform, this is a minor deviation rather than a substantive unfaithfulness.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def apply(df, ctx):
    out = df.copy()
    out["session_log"] = np.log1p(out["session_seconds"].astype(float))
    out.loc[out["session_seconds"].isna(), "session_log"] = float("nan")
    return out

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm


def estimate(df, ctx):
    names = [] + [str(c) for c in ctx.get('covariates', [])]
    core_names = ['converted', 'variant']
    allowed = {*core_names, *('C',)}
    words = lambda c: {
        t
        for t in ''.join(h if h.isalnum() or h in '_' else ' ' for h in c).split()
        if not t.isdigit()
    }
    plain = lambda c: '**' not in c and all(
        h.isalnum() or h in '_ :*+' or ord(h) in (40, 41) for h in c
    )
    names = [
        c
        for c in dict.fromkeys(names)
        if c not in core_names
        and not (words(c) & set(core_names) and words(c) <= allowed and plain(c))
    ]
    used = list(dict.fromkeys(['converted', 'variant', 'user_id'] + names))
    data = df.dropna(subset=used)
    finite = [c for c in used if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    data = data[np.isfinite(data[finite].astype(float)).all(axis=1)]
    hit = data['variant'].astype(str) == 'treatment'
    numeric = pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data['variant'])
    binary = numeric and set(pd.unique(data['variant'])) <= {0, 1}
    if numeric and not binary and not (data['variant'] % 1 == 0).all():
        raise ValueError('the exposure is coded 1 only where variant equals treatment exactly, but variant is a numeric column with fractional values, so one value is not a group; to cut it, code 1 for values at or above the cut after dropping the rows where variant is missing')
    if not hit.any() and not binary:
        raise ValueError(
            'the exposure level ' + 'treatment' + ' is not a value of the column ' + 'variant'
        )
    if hit.any():
        data = data.assign(**{'variant': hit.astype(float)})
    if len(data) and data['variant'].nunique() < 2:
        raise ValueError('the exposure ' + 'variant' + ' has the same value in every row, so it is collinear with the intercept and its effect cannot be estimated: the earlier step that builds it produced a constant. A threshold taken from a numpy median, percentile or quantile is NaN when the column has missing values, and no row then passes it. The pandas median and quantile methods skip missing values')
    core = data[['variant']].astype(float)
    parts = [core]
    numeric = [c for c in names if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    other = [c for c in names if c not in numeric]
    if numeric:
        parts.append(data[numeric].astype(float))
    if other:
        dummies = pd.get_dummies(data[other].astype(str), drop_first=True, dtype=float)
        parts.append(dummies)
    exog = sm.add_constant(pd.concat(parts, axis=1), has_constant='add')
    labels = pd.Series(exog.columns.map(str))
    repeats = labels.groupby(labels).cumcount()
    exog.columns = [f'{c}_repeat{n}' if n else c for c, n in zip(labels, repeats)]
    sources = {f'{c}_{v}': c for c in other for v in data[c].astype(str).unique()}
    target = core.iloc[:, 0].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    floor = 1e-07 * (float(np.abs(target).max()) or 1.0)
    members = {}
    for name in exog.columns:
        members.setdefault(sources.get(str(name)), []).append(name)
    for column in other:
        own = members.get(column, [])
        if not own:
            continue
        span = exog[['const', *own]].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        fitted = span @ np.linalg.lstsq(span, target, rcond=None)[0]
        if float(np.abs(target - fitted).max()) <= floor:
            exog = exog.drop(columns=own)
    protected = ['const', *map(str, core.columns)]
    basis = np.zeros((len(exog), 0))
    aliased = []
    for column in list(exog.columns):
        vector = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(vector))
        residual = vector / size if size else vector
        for _ in range(2):
            residual = residual - basis @ (basis.T @ residual)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(residual))
        if size >= 1e-07:
            basis = np.column_stack([basis, residual / size])
        elif str(column) not in protected:
            aliased.append(str(column))
    kept = [c for c in exog.columns if c not in aliased]
    tangled = []
    for column in aliased:
        target = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        weights = np.linalg.lstsq(exog[kept].to_numpy(dtype=float), target, rcond=None)[0]
        sizes = np.abs(weights) * exog[kept].abs().max().to_numpy(dtype=float)
        floor = 1e-07 * (float(np.abs(target).max()) or 1.0)
        involved = [c for c, size in zip(kept, sizes) if size > floor]
        if any(c in core.columns for c in involved):
            tangled += [c for c in involved if c not in protected]
    tangled = list(dict.fromkeys(tangled))
    exog = exog.drop(columns=aliased + tangled)
    note = 'aliased covariates dropped: ' + ', '.join(aliased) if aliased else ''
    note += '; covariates that rebuild the exposure with them dropped: ' + ', '.join(tangled) if tangled else ''
    endog = data['converted'].astype(float)
    groups = pd.factorize(data['user_id'])[0]
    model = sm.OLS(endog, exog)
    fit = model.fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": groups}, use_t=bool(len(np.unique(groups)) < 30))
    term = 'variant'
    ci = fit.conf_int()
    low, high = (float(v) for v in ci.loc[term])
    value = float(fit.params[term])
    p_value = float(fit.pvalues[term])
    return {
        "estimate": value,
        "ci_low": low,
        "ci_high": high,
        "p_value": p_value,
        "n": int(len(data)),
        "note": note,
    }

option.label: Drop sessions under 5 seconds
option.rationale: Sessions shorter than a few seconds are typically accidental loads, prefetch or crawler hits rather than shoppers; a reviewer would accept a stricter bot threshold chosen from the session_seconds distribution before looking at conversion results, applied identically to both arms.
option.spec: Keep only rows where session_seconds is at least 5.0. Write nothing to ctx. Return the filtered frame.

option.label: Adjust for platform and experiment day
option.rationale: The experiment runs 14 days and platform mix can differ across arms by chance; adjusting for pre-specified covariates that are fixed at randomization and affect conversion is a standard precision and balance check in randomized experiments.
option.spec: Set ctx['covariates'] to ['platform', 'day']. Do not add or drop any columns. Platform is dummy coded by the model step with drop_first=True; day is treated as a numeric covariate. Return the frame unchanged.
option.source: Pre-specified covariate adjustment in A/B testing

option.label: Linear probability model with user-clustered errors, small-sample correction
option.rationale: With clustering on user_id and a binary outcome, the default cluster-robust variance can be anti-conservative or aggressive in finite samples; applying the standard small-sample correction is a defensible inference choice that does not change the point estimate.
option.spec: Fit statsmodels OLS of converted on an intercept and the indicator variant equal to treatment (1 for treatment, 0 for control), plus the covariates in ctx['covariates'] (categorical covariates dummy coded with drop_first=True). Use cluster-robust standard errors clustered on user_id with the small-sample correction (use_correction=True, df_correction=True). Return the coefficient on the variant indicator as the estimate, with its 95% confidence interval and two-sided p-value.
option.source: Cameron and Miller (2015) small-sample cluster correction

data.reason: Dropping sessions under 5 seconds as bot-like is a reasonable, pre-specified stricter threshold chosen from the session_seconds distribution and applied identically to both arms, so it does not leak the outcome. It is an alternative operationalisation of the bot filter (the column note says the threshold is a judgement call), not a change of the estimand, though a reviewer would want a sentence justifying the 5 s cut-off.

The option keeps the conventional linear probability model with user-clustered errors and only adds the small-sample correction (HC1-style df adjustment) to the cluster-robust variance; it does not change the point estimate, the estimand, or the covariates. With 16,000 user clusters the correction is nearly immaterial, but it is a standard, defensible inference choice for a binary outcome in an LPM.

Platform and experiment day are fixed at randomisation (platform is set per session and day is the experiment calendar), so they are pre-treatment covariates; adjusting for them is a standard precision and balance check in randomised experiments and does not change the estimand, since the difference in conversion between arms is still the target. Day is numeric as a simple trend control, which is acceptable for 14 levels, and the option does not alter rows.

data.problem: The spec asks for cluster-robust standard errors on user_id with the small-sample correction (use_correction=True, df_correction=True), but the code calls fit with cov_type='cluster' and only uses t-based inference when fewer than 30 clusters, so the default cluster correction applies and there is no explicit use_correction/df_correction setting. The code also drops rows with missing values and filters to finite numeric values before the model, which is complete-case handling and acceptable. The mismatch is in the covariance correction settings relative to the spec.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def apply(df, ctx):
    out = df.copy()
    out["session_log"] = np.log1p(out["session_seconds"].astype(float))
    out.loc[out["session_seconds"].isna(), "session_log"] = float("nan")
    return out

        "ci_low": float(row["Conf. Int. Low"]),
        "ci_high": float(row["Cont. Int. Hi."]),
        "p_value": float(row["Pr(>|z|)"]),
        "n": int(len(data)),
        "note": note,
        "extra": {"std_err": float(row["Std. Err."])},
    }

options.label: Linear probability model with user-clustered errors, small-sample correction
options.rationale: With clustering on user_id and a binary outcome, the default cluster-robust variance can be anti-conservative or aggressive in finite samples; applying the standard small-sample correction is a defensible inference choice that does not change the point estimate.
options.spec: Fit statsmodels OLS of converted on an intercept and the indicator variant equal to treatment (1 for treatment, 0 for control), plus the covariates in ctx['covariates'] (categorical covariates dummy coded with drop_first=True). Use cluster-robust standard errors clustered on user_id with the small-sample correction (use_correction=True, df_correction=True). Return the coefficient on the variant indicator as the estimate, with its 95% confidence interval and two-sided p-value.
options.source: Cameron, Gelbach & Miller (2011), Robust inference with multiway clustering; Imbens & Kolesár (2016) on small-sample cluster inference
options.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm


def estimate(df, ctx):
    covariates = [str(c) for c in ctx.get('covariates', [])]
    names = [c for c in dict.fromkeys(covariates) if c not in ('converted', 'variant', 'user_id')]
    used = list(dict.fromkeys(['converted', 'variant', 'user_id'] + names))
    data = df.dropna(subset=used).copy()
    hit = data['variant'].astype(str) == 'treatment'
    if hit.any():
        data['variant'] = hit.astype(float)
    else:
        data['variant'] = pd.to_numeric(data['variant'], errors='coerce').astype(float)
    if data['variant'].nunique() < 2:
        raise ValueError('the exposure variant has the same value in every row')
    parts = [data[['variant']].astype(float)]
    numeric = [c for c in names if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    other = [c for c in names if c not in numeric]
    if numeric:
        parts.append(data[numeric].astype(float))
    if other:
        parts.append(pd.get_dummies(data[other].astype(str), drop_first=True, dtype=float))
    exog = sm.add_constant(pd.concat(parts, axis=1), has_constant='add')
    exog = exog.loc[:, ~exog.columns.duplicated()]
    endog = data['converted'].astype(float)
    groups = pd.factorize(data['user_id'])[0]
    fit = sm.OLS(endog, exog).fit(
        cov_type='cluster',
        cov_kwds={'groups': groups, 'use_correction': True, 'df_correction': True},
        use_t=True,
    )
    ci = fit.conf_int()
    low, high = (float(v) for v in ci.loc['variant'])
    return {
        'estimate': float(fit.params['variant']),
        'ci_low': low,
        'ci_high': high,
        'p_value': float(fit.pvalues['variant']),
        'n': int(len(data)),
    }

report.narrative: The original analysis estimated -0.141 (95% CI -0.495 to 0.212, p = 0.43, n = 29,587) and returned the verdict DON'T SHIP. No minimal flip was found: no defensible combination of choices reverses the verdict, so there is no flip to re-execute. The decisions that move the estimate are the bot filter and, to a much smaller degree, the covariate adjustment. Dropping sessions under 2 seconds or under 5 seconds shifts the estimate toward zero, to about -0.128 to -0.136, and widens or shifts the interval slightly. Adding platform or experiment day as covariates changes it by only about 0.001. The choice of estimator makes no visible difference: the logit average marginal effect reproduces the baseline exactly, and the small-sample linear probability model gives the same result as the baseline. Across the 18 distinct results from the 19 universes, the estimates stay within a narrow band around the baseline, and every confidence interval includes zero. The judge accepted the planner's main options: dropping internal sessions, keeping all session lengths, adjusting for platform, and the user-clustered linear probability model. It rejected keeping internal sessions, because that departs from the genuine-session estimand. Robustness: 100% of the analysis grid agrees with the original verdict and 0% reverses it.
caveats: The option 'Winsorize session_seconds at the 1st and 99th percentiles' of the step 'How to handle extreme session lengths' failed its smoke run and is not in the analysis (line 8: np.percentile(...) returns NaN when the column has a missing value, and every comparison with NaN is False, so a threshold built from it marks no row; u).
19 universes ran but only 18 gave distinct results; universes with identical results are counted once in the robustness share.

The option 'Logit with average marginal effect' (estimate) is a no-op: it gives the same result as the baseline in every universe it appears in (estimate, confidence interval and n equal to 6 significant digits), so it is not a different analysis. It is excluded from the robustness share and from the flip search.

The 100% robustness estimate is the share of the analysis grid that agrees with the original verdict; it was sampled as follows: the whole grid: 18 combinations, 18 distinct results; exact, not sampled, and independent of the beam search. The universes the beam search explored are the ones closest to flipping, so their own agreement share leans toward flips and is not used as the estimate.
